Medical History

- Current health concerns and risk factors: 3-day history of severe “blinding” headache (8/10) worst over right eye; photophobia; transient “shooting-light” visual disturbance; mild nausea; partial relief with ibuprofen. Uses combined oral contraceptive pill (OCP)—risk factor for migraine/CVST.
- Relevant family medical history: Mother has migraines with vomiting; no other conditions recorded.
- Medications (including OTC or shared medications): Combined oral contraceptive pill (brand not documented) – dose/route/frequency not documented; Ibuprofen PRN; Paracetamol advised – dose/route/frequency not documented. Allergies: none reported.
- Immunisation status reviewed: Not recorded.
- Sexual and reproductive health: On estrogen-containing OCP started 1 yr ago; no side-effects reported; no STI/obstetric history recorded.
- Physical activity and nutrition: Not recorded.
- Alcohol, tobacco, and substance use: Non-smoker; alcohol ≈3 drinks once weekly; denies recreational drugs.
- Hearing loss or concerns: Not recorded.
- Mood/mental health (including depression, self-harm risk): Reports low energy likely secondary to headache; no mood disorder or self-harm risk discussed.
- Vision problems or recent changes: Photophobia and transient visual phenomena; recent optometry check reportedly normal.
- Family and social relationships, caring responsibilities: Lives alone; works from home; has missed work due to headaches.

Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

Key findings: First episode of prolonged unilateral severe headache with photophobia and visual disturbance in young woman on estrogen OCP; no focal neurologic signs, fever, or infection.

Working diagnosis: Probable migraine with visual aura (status migrainosus).

Differential diagnoses:  
• Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis – OCP use, persistent positional headache; serious cause to exclude.  
• Idiopathic intracranial hypertension – young female, visual symptoms; requires fundoscopic evaluation.  
Lower likelihood: tension headache, subarachnoid hemorrhage, intracranial mass (monitor for red flags).

Plan:  
• Arrange urgent face-to-face review for full neurological exam, fundoscopy, and blood pressure measurement.  
• Prescribe stronger NSAID (agent not specified) plus paracetamol; advise taking with food.  
• Review suitability of current OCP; consider alternative contraception if migraine with aura confirmed.  
• Safety-net: attend ED if pain becomes unbearable, changes character, or neurological symptoms develop.

Management Plan

- Medication: Stronger NSAID prescribed; continue/alternate with paracetamol (both dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Appointment: Book in-person consultation via support team for neuro exam, fundoscopy, and BP check.
- Contraception review: Reassess OCP at next visit; possible change if migraine with aura confirmed.
- Education: Medication to be taken with food; monitor symptoms; seek urgent care if worsening.
- Follow-up: Face-to-face appointment scheduled; cancel if symptoms fully resolve beforehand.

Consider:

- Allied health referral (EPC – 10 visits): Not recorded.
- Reproductive or sexual health clinic referral: Not recorded (may be required if OCP change needed).
- Mental health support if indicated (e.g., psychologist, AMS support): Not recorded.
- CTG registration: Not recorded.
- Preventive health follow-up booked (e.g., flu vaccine, Pap test): Not recorded.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Migraine with visual aura – High likelihood: Unilateral severe headache, photophobia, aura-like visual disturbance, positive family history, partial response to NSAID.  
2. Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis – Moderate likelihood: Female on estrogen OCP, new persistent headache, positional component.  
3. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension – Moderate likelihood: Young woman on OCP with visual symptoms; needs fundoscopy for papilledema.

● Missing clinically expected elements: Vital signs (BP, HR, temp), anthropometrics (height/weight/BMI/waist), immunisation history, urinalysis, detailed diet/exercise history, formal mental-health screening.  
● No transcript–DDx contradictions identified.  
● Transcript quality: Generally clear; some audio gaps (patient name, pill brand, exact alcohol quantity) and lack of demographic details.
